source.title: Refining Positive and Toxic Samples for Dual Safety Self-Alignment of LLMs With Minimal Human Interventions
source.authors: Jing-Xian Xu; Guo-Shun Nan; Sheng Guan; Si-Cong Leng; Yilian Liu; Zixiao Wang; Yuyang Ma; Zhi-li Zhou; Yan-Zhao Hou; Xiao-Feng Tao

record.file_problem: Some figure text and labels are garbled in the supplied text; the main text and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper proposes and evaluates a safety fine-tuning method using positive responses and toxic responses as unlikelihood-training targets. Its safety behavior is deliberately induced by that training, so the results do not test whether ordinary harmful or benign fine-tuning erodes existing safety, whether safety is concentrated in early tokens or few parameters, or whether a compliant opening bypasses safety.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates its own safety-alignment method, including safety benchmark scores and an AutoDAN attack evaluation. These are outcomes of a method intended to induce safety, not measurements of the claim’s proposed safety-degradation mechanism. No labels are assigned because relation is not tests. The paper cites prior work on safety degradation from fine-tuning; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes PT-ALIGN, a safety-alignment method that pairs MLE on safe responses with token-level unlikelihood training on toxic responses, and reports only that method's safety gains. It never fine-tunes an aligned model on harmful or benign data to measure safety loss (V1, V2). It measures no per-token KL or position effects (V3). It runs no prefill or opening-token attack (V4). It does no parameter localization (V5) and no analysis of why safety is shallow (V6). Its token-level unlikelihood skips the shared leading tokens of positive and toxic pairs to avoid penalising safe tokens; this is not a test of spreading safety beyond the opening (V7). The claim appears only as motivation, citing Qi et al. [14]. The method neither relies on nor tests the shallow-alignment finding, so cites_only/T6 fits better than the reader's uses_without_test/T4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that PT-ALIGN improves the safety of the tested LLMs with fewer than 50 human annotations, while keeping helpfulness and general performance. They attribute the gains to the stark safety contrast between positive and toxic samples.
record.recipe_differences: PT-ALIGN synthesizes paired safe and toxic responses and trains with MLE plus token-level unlikelihood loss. The paper does not reproduce the original harmful-fine-tuning intervention or measure per-token KL concentration.
record.method_sensitivity: In PT-ALIGN experiments, the reported harmless score rises as the sample count increases from 2,000 to 16,000; the authors report the best results around λ = 0.4, with slight declines at higher or lower tested values. They state that seed-set variation did not significantly affect performance.

fits_no_version.finding: PT-ALIGN (MLE plus fine-grained unlikelihood training on self-generated safe/toxic pairs) lowers harm scores and raises harmlessness and preference accuracy across 8 models. It also reduces AutoDAN ASR on LLaMA2-13B to 0.51%, versus 5.06% for LLaMA2-13B-chat.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlikelihood training on self-synthesized toxic responses improves safety benchmark scores and jailbreak resistance relative to SFT, DPO and KTO on the same data.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the benchmark results in the supplied text. Several table entries are reported as score changes without absolute pre-training values. Some figure text is garbled in the supplied extraction. The paper reports its proposed alignment method’s outcomes, not an uncontrolled harmful-fine-tuning degradation test.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted helpfulness, honesty, other HHH, general-capability, detailed seed-set, and penalty-coefficient outcomes because they do not measure any claim version; the seed and penalty-coefficient results are summarized in method_sensitivity. Also omitted case-study text examples and loss-curve comparisons, which do not report a claim-version measure.

untested.parts: No ordinary fine-tuning on harmful examples; toxic samples are used only as unlikelihood targets.
No benign fine-tuning of an aligned model followed by a harmful-compliance measurement.
No per-token KL or position-wise comparison of aligned and base models.
No prefilling, adversarial-suffix or decoding attacks. AutoDAN is not framed as getting past the opening tokens.
LoRA is used for training, but no test of whether safety is localized in few weights or ranks.
No analysis of whether data or objective causes shallowness.
No measurement of safety depth across response positions. Skipping shared prefix tokens in unlikelihood loss is not a deepening intervention.

record.verdict_notes: Safety behaviour here is deliberately induced by the authors' own training. No result bears on how shallow existing alignment is or whether fine-tuning erodes it. The text mentions 9 LLMs, but Tables II and III together cover 8. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether ordinary fine-tuning on harmful examples causes a safety-trained model to comply; toxic responses are used with unlikelihood training to discourage their generation.
Does not test whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning raises harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence or compare aligned and base models across response positions.

Does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as ways to bypass safety. AutoDAN is evaluated, but it is not presented as a test of getting past early response tokens.
LoRA is used for training, but the paper does not test whether a small set of parameters or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether the data or objective produces safety shallowness.
Does not test whether training that spreads safety beyond early tokens deepens safety or whether such deepening holds up.

rows.check: LLaMA2-13B-chat AutoDAN ASR (5.06%) is a comparator for the paper's own method. AutoDAN is a rewritten jailbreak prompt, not a compliant-opening prefill or suffix test of V4. No no-attack ASR is given, so it cannot show attack-induced erosion.
